Visit
viz'it
v. (to come to with a purpose, in blessing or in judgment; rendering Hebrew paqad, Greek episkeptomai)
From the Latin visito, to go to see, from video, to see. Hebrew paqad is far stronger than the English social sense: it means to attend to, to muster, to reckon with — a visitation is an inspection with consequences.

Biblical Definition

To visit in Scripture is to come with a purpose and to act, and the same word covers mercy and judgment. In mercy: “the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken” (Genesis 21:1) — the visitation is Isaac, and the verse repeats as he had said and as he had spoken because the point is a promise kept after twenty-five years and a laugh. Zacharias uses it of the incarnation: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68) — God visiting in person, after four hundred silent years. In judgment the same verb: “I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me” (Exodus 20:5). The qualifier matters — of them that hate me — and the next verse promises mercy unto thousands of them that love him, so the ratio is not symmetrical. Then James turns the word toward the church's duty and makes it the test of religion: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (James 1:27). We are to visit as God visits — going to people, in their affliction, and doing something.

Webster 1828 Definition

To come with purpose and act — in mercy or in judgment. The LORD visited Sarah, visited and redeemed his people in Christ, visits iniquity on those who hate him; and pure religion visits the fatherless and widows.

expand to see more

VISIT, v.t. [L. visito, from video, to see.] To go or come to see; to attend; as, to visit a friend.

2. To go or come to see for inspection, examination, correction of abuses; as, to visit the churches.

3. To send good or evil to, as a punishment or blessing; to bless or afflict.

4. In Scripture, to send judgments; I will visit their transgression with the rod, Ps. 89.

5. Also, to come to in mercy; the Lord visited Sarah, Gen. 21.

Key Scripture

Genesis 21:1 — "And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken."

Exodus 20:5 — "Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;"

Luke 7:16 — "And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people."

James 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Modern Corruption

Exodus 20:5 is read as God punishing children for their parents' sins, ignoring the clause that limits it — while James 1:27 is quoted for social action detached from the second half of the same verse.

expand to see more

Exodus 20:5 is a favourite text of objectors and is regularly quoted without its qualifier. The visiting falls on them that hate me — that is, on children who continue in their fathers' hatred of God, not on innocents charged with ancestral guilt. Scripture states the individual principle elsewhere with no ambiguity: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20). What the second commandment describes is the observable fact that sin runs in households, that idolatry is taught by example, and that a generation may inherit its parents' hatred along with their furniture. And the promise attached is far larger than the threat: mercy unto thousands of them that love God and keep his commandments. James 1:27 has the opposite problem. It is enlisted for programmes of social concern with its second clause quietly dropped, though the verse defines pure religion as both visiting the afflicted and keeping oneself unspotted from the world. A church that does one and abandons the other has not obeyed half the verse; it has failed the definition.

The principle to recover is that God's visiting is the model for ours. He does not send word to Sarah; he visits her. He does not merely pity his people; he visits and redeems them in the flesh. James therefore uses the same verb for orphans and widows, and the choice is deliberate. Visiting in the biblical sense is bodily presence with intent to act — going to where the affliction is, at cost, and doing something about it. It cannot be done at a distance and it cannot be delegated to an institution without ceasing to be what the word means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew paqad is to attend to, muster, appoint, or reckon with — hence to visit in blessing or judgment. Greek episkeptomai is to look upon, to care for; the root of episkopos, overseer.

expand to see more

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, muster, attend to, punish; the great verb of divine visitation.

Hebrew pequddah (H6486) — visitation, oversight, reckoning; the day of visitation.

Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to look upon, visit, care for; James 1:27 and Matthew 25:36.

Greek episkope (G1984) — visitation, oversight; the time of thy visitation, Luke 19:44.

Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, bishop; one whose office is to visit and inspect.

Usage

"Of a promise kept: the LORD visited Sarah as he had said (Genesis 21:1)."

"Of the incarnation: he hath visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68)."

"Of the test of pure religion: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction (James 1:27)."
